title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
source: Axios — Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels (2026-11-17)
body: One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership. Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership. The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios. Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes , a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic. Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision. Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings. Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals. The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress. One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference. Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes. "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal. Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October. A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals. The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in. But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation. "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said. What they're saying: Freedom Caucus members oppose Main Street's proposal. "It's not going to happen," outgoing HFC Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Axios. "They introduce it every year." "That's inappropriate," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga) told Axios of Flood's original proposal. Clyde also told Axios he doesn't think the proposal will get anywhere, saying that he thinks enough feel the same as he does to kill it. Reality check: With Republicans headed into one of the smallest minorities in recent history, the changes would have little effect in the upcoming Congress. But members want to settle the conference's accountability rules now, so when they regain the majority, the same divisions won't threaten to derail their agenda. "This is us simply setting the table so that when we do return to the majority, we can do so built on a foundation that addresses some of the hiccups we experienced during the 119th Congress," Flood told Axios. "We're in the minority now, this is the time to set the rules. This is the time to get this thing right," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. "The goal is to take away the ability of an extremely small group to extort leadership," the member added. "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.
